I get about eleven of these a month, and I am honest with the teams about how I read them. I read the first paragraph, I read anything marked outstanding, and I read the variance table. That is four minutes. If your bad news is on page three, I will find it in the meeting instead of in the report, and by then I am annoyed and you have lost the chance to frame it. The reports I trust most are the ones where the worst line is near the top, written in plain words, with the action in the same paragraph. Something like: the equipment base has not been signed off, the client review is now scheduled for the ninth, and the drawings have been re-sequenced so that the steel package is not affected. That is three sentences. I know the problem, the date and the mitigation, and I do not need to call anybody.

Every line in that report was true, and that was the problem. Month one said the layout was progressing. Month two said the layout was progressing. In month three somebody asked a direct question and we found out that the layout had been waiting for a soil report since week two. Nothing had been hidden. Nobody had lied. The word progressing had just been doing a lot of work for two months. Since then I ask for one thing in every report, and it takes ten seconds to write. If an item has not moved since the last report, say so, and say what it is waiting for. Not progressing. Waiting for the soil report, requested on the fourteenth, chased twice. A reader can do something with that sentence. A reader can do nothing at all with progressing.
